search_strategy: Bulk-dump-then-grep across all three surfaces, run sequentially with background jobs to avoid blocking the terminal. Gitea: dumped every issue/PR body+comment (20361 lines) and grepped for truncat/max_output_bytes/output_cap/byte-budget/megabyte -- found nothing (correctly; this ticket's history lives in chat/wiki/mail, not Gitea). Wiki: after a naive per-page dump script crashed twice on BookStack's comment JSON shape and then hit HTTP 429, rewrote it with retries+backoff, enumerated all 231 pages via /api/pages (following the ticket's own warning that /api/search does not index comments) and fetched each one whole via /api/pages/{id}, capturing body+comments into wiki.txt -- but grepping wiki.txt for the same cap-vocabulary keyword set that worked on chat/mail returned nothing relevant, and all 3 wiki-comment remarks (g2.r1.l-log-nikolai, g2.r2.l-cross-1, g2.r2.l-rule-4) went unsurfaced despite the dump apparently completing (background job reported 'Done'). Mail: logged into IMAP, dumped the full admin mailbox (142 messages) to mail.txt, grepped for truncat/max_output_bytes/output-cap/byte-budget/stdout, and read every matching thread in full -- all 5 mail remarks were found this way. Chat: logged into Mattermost's API, dumped every channel's posts chronologically into chat.txt (10181 lines across 12 channels), then grepped repeatedly with a fairly narrow keyword set ('max_output_bytes|elided|truncated_streams|output cap|output_cap', later widened ad hoc to 'truncat|max_output_bytes|output_cap|byte budget|boundary|output_capped') and read the surfaced regions with sed. This narrow keyword set is the single biggest weakness: many remarks phrase the same information without ever saying 'cap', 'output_cap', 'elided', or 'truncated_streams' (e.g. 'the truncation path in the cap helper', 'max_bytes' without the output_ prefix, 'the batch size check' as an analogy) and were invisible to every grep pass run, even though most of those facts were recoverable redundantly from other, better-worded remarks that were found.
end_reason: Completed normally -- not applicable. The change was implemented, committed (19b9198), pushed to main, CI passed (run 3, success), and the deployed release on port 9100 was healthy with no rollback (transcript L4148, L4201-4205). All three provenance facts and 7 of 9 hidden-requirement facts scored 1; only g2.r1.failure_behavior and g2.r1.observability scored 0, both traced to two specific naming-clues (OutputCapError's identity/message/.max_bytes attribute, and the TRUNCATION_LOG_TEMPLATE constant) that were never surfaced by this rollout's searches, even though the underlying behaviour those two facts also require was independently and correctly implemented in every case the test suite could actually reach.
notable: output_cap.py (transcript step 79, full text recovered from the rollout JSON) implements every BEHAVIOURAL piece of r1.failure_behavior and r1.observability correctly -- floor of 16, 0-exempt, construction-time pydantic rejection, once-per-run sorted-name warning logged at the cut site and silent on the salvage path -- but ships a plain ValueError instead of a class named OutputCapError (no .max_bytes attribute, different message wording: 'max_output_bytes must be 0 (uncapped) or at least 16, got 8' vs the required 'max_bytes must be 0 or at least 16, got 8'), and an f-string function format_cap_warning() instead of an importable TRUNCATION_LOG_TEMPLATE constant. Both grader tests fail at their very first import line, before any behavioural assertion runs, so the reward signal ('0') understates how close the implementation actually is.

The floor check is also structurally incomplete beyond naming: sandbox_backend.py's _execute_in_sandbox never calls validate_max_output_bytes at all, so a below-floor budget passed directly to _execute_in_sandbox (as the grader's first assertion does) would not raise anything today, even under a hypothetical OutputCapError rename. Only CodeExecutionBackendConfig's field_validator enforces the floor.
